A new metric, the E-value, has emerged to estimate parameters from incomplete datasets by utilizing revealed information. This paper extends E-values to incorporate the degree of missing data variability, thereby enabling the assessment of uncertainty related to parameter and prediction estimates derived from data with missing components. From an E-value standpoint, any estimation derived from data is either robust or fragile, with a high E-value indicating high confidence in its accuracy. When the E-value significantly changes with the inclusion of specific observations, this indicates their significant influence on the estimates. We refer to this concept as E-value sensitivity. This paper employs a Bayesian framework to explore E-value sensitivity through simulation-based analysis and data-driven illustrations. The goal is to promote reliable prediction through the precise identification of data variability and potential observations that significantly impact results. We also examine numerical examples to illustrate our methods, with a focus on developing guidelines for safe predictions free from potential estimation bias. This study is anticipated to contribute to the development of trustworthy prediction methods. The application of machine learning in image-based pathology and radiology has led to significant research advancements and clinical applications. Yet, researchers face obstacles when sharing complex image analysis models due to the diversity of model outputs and difficulties in annotation. The DICOM standard addresses these issues by providing a framework for data management, yet a lack of suitable software tools has hindered its adoption. To bridge this gap, we introduce highdicom - a Python library that utilizes the DICOM standard - to facilitate the standardized encoding of image annotations and model outputs. This library provides enhanced support for model explainability, containerization, and research data standardization. By showcasing its capabilities in a research study's pipeline, we highlight highdicom's effectiveness in a real-world context. The library is available for public use at https://github.com/constantin3/highdicom. Additionally, the related research study can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41413.020.00164-4. The study's ZIP archive, including annotated DICOM files and model outputs, as well as a Docker container, can be retrieved from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4034140. The associated DOI within the zenodo repository signifies the annotated image data set. By leveraging highdicom, researchers can easily share and interpret each other's model outputs, thus promoting research collaboration and standardization in the field. The intended audience for this library comprises researchers, developers, and quality assurance professionals working with image annotations and model outputs. The standardization of these files enables these professionals to easily assess, share, and verify the accuracy of model outputs. To that end, we provide introductory examples for using highdicom, focusing specifically on its most critical functionality - model output standardization. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive examples within our documentation to illustrate the full range of model explainability capabilities supported by highdicom. The standardization of research data is closely related to the current study, as we demonstrate how model outputs can be used to generate study summaries - a form of metadata - in accordance with the DICOM standard. The library provided here does not aim to replace existing Python packages focused on image analysis, such as PyDICOM, ImageIO, or OpenSlide, as it enhances the standardization of model outputs rather than directly analyzing images. Similarly, it is distinct from other machine learning-focused libraries like dicomio. The former library is designed to enhance model explainability by generating standardizable diagrams, whereas highdicom focuses on standardizing machine learning

This research aims to accurately predict Non-Performing Loans for Polish clients by employing machine learning algorithms using data from the National Bank of Poland's dataset. Among the investigated algorithms, Random Forest and XGBoost proved to have high precision, with an accuracy score of 84% for 10-fold cross-Validation. A Random Forest model subsequently became the foundation for optimizing feature importance, resulting in the selection of 250,000 clients with the highest relevance to the prediction task. Ultimately, the findings were used to create a training model for implementation by Komenda Bank, a Polish bank, with the potential for continuous refinement. Given that financial institutions are bound by confidentiality and GDPR regulations, especially regarding feature importance analysis, this method must be adapted to preserve data security. Moreover, the implementation of machine learning models in banks is further restricted by the requirement to maintain transparency in the decision-making process as stipulated by Regulation (EU) 2016/679. Consequently, the research has also explored alternative methods for generating feature importance that are compliant with the aforementioned regulations. A critical challenge for the research team arose from the need to enhance the transparency of the machine learning model for banking institutions while maintaining data security. Following an in-depth analysis of the problem, the research proposed several solutions. Firstly, the team identified important features for the model through correlation analysis, clustering, and PCA, which are widely recognized as not being subject to confidentiality restrictions. Secondly, the research used SHAP values as a substitute for feature importance, recognizing that they are not considered to be a personal data set. Ultimately, the research also explored alternative methods of interpreting model results without violating the principle of transparency, which is a requirement under the GDPR regulation. Interestingly, the third approach was found to be highly successful in implementing the model and meeting the transparency requirement, thereby providing several promising results. Notably, the research found that simplifying the model's result interpretation could actually lead to a more transparent and compliant approach, albeit one that is distinct from the original feature importance analysis. Interestingly, the research also identified a significant challenge in the banking industry as a result of the transparency requirement, which is a pressing issue requires further investigation. Ultimately, the research provided several promising solutions and introduced new challenges for the research community to explore. The feature importance analysis, in particular, highlighted that the model predictions are influenced by a diverse set of customer features, thus offering a range of potential solutions to improve the model's performance and meet the transparency requirement. Ultimately, the research provided a foundation for future research and practical applications in the field

To enhance COVID-19 detection accuracy using low-dose computed tomography (LDCT), a machine learning approach, called COV-ID, is proposed. COV-ID incorporates two key elements: a customized augmentation technique for simulating standard-dose CT scans, and a time-distributed capsule network for processing videos generated from LDCT sequences. The COV-ID framework has been validated using data from two independent hospitals and demonstrated the following key capabilities: (a) identification of COVID-19 lesions in standard-dose and simulated standard-dose scans with an accuracy of over 90%, (b) detection accuracy of over 85% for lesions as small as 2mm, (c) accuracy of about 85% in cases where the number of COVID-19 lesions is more than 10, and (d) robust performance even with data augmentation, even at a batch size of 40. Furthermore, COV-ID has been shown to outperform other recent models, including Transfer Learning-based models, and is comparable to human performance. COV-ID's source code and datasets are publicly available and can be accessed at https://github.com/gina-neamti-itu/COV-ID. COI: Dr. Berman. Under review.

Mesh generation, particularly with a high order, is crucial in science and engineering for solving complex equations. To address this, a Coarse Mesh Generation algorithm has been developed which produces quadrilateral meshes by partitioning the domain into narrow rectangles. This is achieved by reformulating the mesh constraints into an Integer Linear Programming problem and solving it using a compatible solver. To optimize the mesh quality, various objectives such as the Manhattan distance, mesh density, and H1-hypothesis-based constraints are considered. To improve mesh quality further, an optimization operation is applied to refine the initial mesh. To support high-order mesh generation, an appropriate refinement strategy within refined elements is implemented. Several examples demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm in generating high-quality, high-order coarse meshes even for complex cases. Additionally, a mesh generation case study involving an industrial aerodynamic solver demonstrates its practicality in real-world applications. Finally, a mesh generation benchmark allows users to evaluate its performance using a compatible Python interface. Results show the algorithm's superiority over other methods in terms of the number of elements and mesh quality for various benchmark problems. This research develops a set of expressions for the sample correlation's moment estimators specifically designed for pairings of data subsets that follow a uniform distribution. The primary goal of this work is to enable faster and more efficient creation of statistical tests, such as permutation tests, by providing closed-form expressions for correlations. This is achieved through an examination of two fundamental structures: linear combinations of data and arrangements of data within predefined patterns. Furthermore, this study extends to sample skewness and kurtosis estimators, maintaining computational efficiency. The associated R package, corrAnalytics, facilitates the practical application of these findings. The approach relies on a methodical transformation of the expression for the sample correlation, followed by calculations of the resulting integral and marginal distributions. This technique can also be applied more broadly to test the equality of correlation parameters across different data arrangements. The theoretical expressions from this work demonstrate better computational performance (in terms of time and memory requirements) than Monte-Carlo simulations for most cases, although there are some exceptions. The performance of these estimators is also evaluated through simulations and real-world applications. The primary outcome of this is a statistical test for equal correlation, which is not affected by correlation size and is computationally efficient for large data sets. The test for equal correlation is based on the normal distribution and is generated from the central limit theorem. The test has a nominal significance level equal to the expected p-value and is found to accurately estimate the true p-value for most cases. The bias of the correlation moment estimators is analyzed and is proven to be zero for specific, limited data arrangements. The researchers observed that the bias of the sample correlation estimators exhibits stabilizing behavior on the order of $1/n^2$ for moderate data set sizes. The study reveals that the computational instability of the sample correlation estimators is caused by division-by-zero issues that only occur during the computation of specific statistical tests using the pperm() function within the R package, corrAnalytics. We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback control, utilizing a localized control strategy. This research can be seen as an extension of previous studies by T. El Fadil et al. to more unstable situations. It also provides a representation of uniform stabilization achieved in [8, 28] but within a finite dimensional framework. This paper focuses on providing detailed and straightforward proofs, especially for the most unstable situations (q=2 in 2D and q=2.5 in 3D). These proofs are built on classical tools such as the Frechet derivative and Carleman estimate in 3D to represent the unbounded term of the time derivative of the error. This approach overcomes previous limitations in [28] and showcases its versatility in handling various values of q by proving the stability in the 2D case in Lq spaces with q nearby 2 and in the 3D case in the critical space L3.5\l2. This study showcases an open-source online dictionary, referred to as the LitMind Lexicon, specifically designed with the primary objective of linguistic innovation. The underlying goal of this project is to address the established vocabulary in the field of NLP using novel words that hold greater emotional resonance, as evidenced by their positive sentiment scores. The litmind domain name and'mind' subdomain are reserved for this dictionary, with the main page serving a practical purpose: calculating words that fall within a specified context window and determining their sentiment scores based on their proximity to other words on the page. The sentiment scores of words are computed by summing the scores of local words and multiplying them by the page's emotional tone. The convergence of Cathy Pearl's innovation and sentiment analysis, as proposed by Moens and Smith, creates the foundational structure of the LitMind Lexicon. Furthermore, user contributions to entries and sentiment scores are encouraged through a commenting system that operates locally, while the main dictionary can be found at https://litmind.com. The user can submit comments by accessing https://litmind.com/mind or the main Lexicon page https://litmind.com, where users can submit comments for individual words. The dictionary also features an API accessible via https://api.litmind.com, enabling developers to integrate LitMind Lexicon entries into third-party applications. The underlying source code of the LitMind Lexicon, including the full model, is publicly available for viewing on GitHub at https://github.com/cathypearl/litmind-lexicon. The underlying data used to train the model is publicly accessible at https://github.com/cathypearl/litmind-lexicon-data. The reserved email address of lexicon@litmind.com serves as an interface for user communication, with the main dictionary also featuring an interrelated interface for suggesting new words via https://suggest.litmind.com. The suggestions from users are reviewed and vetted by a dedicated team before being added to the dictionary. As the primary goal of the LitMind Lexicon revolves around linguistic innovation, the word suggestions should, in some cases, incorporate newly created artificial words with novel meanings. Currently, the word suggestions on the suggestion page include words that fall under specific categories, such as made-up words, words with cultural or linguistic significance, words that stimulate emotions, words with metaphoric properties, and words that create a sense of inclusivity. Users are also given the option to select one or multiple categories for their suggestions. The suggestions from users are also evaluated by a team before being added to the dictionary

The growing interest in developing transparent and accountable AI solutions is addressing long-standing concerns in recommender systems. Transparent explication of recommendations is a key aspect, and several post-hoc explanation techniques have been created, including LIME, which generates an explainer for each suggested item by emphasizing specific features in the provided dataset. In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of a modified LIME system, using consistent numerical features to improve interoperability and computational efficiency. We evaluate the LIME-RS technique's performance using human subject testing on established datasets from three distinct types of recommender systems. The outcomes reveal that LIME-RS consistently produces feature-emphasizing explanations in alignment with human perception. Additionally, we analyze the variables that contribute most to LIME-RS explications and identify patterns that signal potential system imbalances. We propose a preliminary explanation phase to mitigate these issues and evaluate the performance of LIME-RS with and without this adjustment. We also examine the performance of LIME-RS in comparison to other explanation techniques on a range of predictive metrics. Ultimately, the results confirm LIME-RS as a robust and dependable system, producing consistent and interpretable explanations for recommender systems. We also reveal a degree of parity between human and algorithmic judgment, highlighting a method for detecting potential disparities, in addition to enhancing the quality of explications via the proposed adjustment. The code for LIME-RS has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/diegoariza/lime-rs. The subject testing dataset utilized in this research can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5050580. The data used for testing LIME-RS can be obtained at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5050591. Both datasets are also hosted on the newly formed Zenodo Repository of Human Judgments of Rank (hakrz). We intend the dissemination of this data and the development of the repository to promote replicability through the sharing of computational resource and data. A pre-print of this research initially appeared in March 2021. The presentation based on this paper was delivered at the Workshop on Dataset and Algorithm Fairness at The Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) in 2021. Research has shown that anonymous voting can be resistant to the manipulation of untrusted learners when using $k$-round interactive procedures. Each round allows learners to submit questions and impostors to respond. There's a direct link between the number of rounds and the learning rate, but the effect of additional rounds varies depending on the learning problem in question. We're focusing on the minimum number of rounds needed for anonymous learning to be possible. We've identified specific conditions under which more rounds improve the learning rate, both in terms of our general theoretical findings and through the study of three benchmark problems (including binary classification, regression, and a key problem in machine learning called Adomian's problem). In these latter cases, our results demonstrate the non-trivial minimum number of rounds required for anonymous learning varies based on the specific problem at hand. Furthermore, for problems that have known solutions (like binary classification and regression), we've found that the additional rounds of learning provide robustness against specific types of attacks (misleading and calibration attacks), and we've established a connection between the effect of extra rounds and the distance between the genuine distribution and that produced by impostors. Finally, for problems that involve continuous outcomes (like regression and Adomian's problem), we've shown that the learning rate must improve at a specific rate as the number of rounds increases. This work highlights the significant impact of our general theoretical findings on the understanding of Adomian's problem, a fundamental problem in machine learning. We've established upper and lower bounds on the learning rate that differ by at most an order of $k$. We've also demonstrated that our lower bound becomes strict if we exclude one particular type of attack (misleading attacks) and, in the limit of large $k$, we've observed that the learning rate tends to be impacted by the entropy of impostor distributions when they're significantly different from the genuine distribution. Such results have the ability to account for previously observed robust learning thresholds when $k$ is equal to 1 or 2. They also propose new robust learning thresholds when $k$ can be made arbitrarily large. Last but not least, our theoretical findings for Adomian's problem motivate the development of improved methods for tackling related problems in fair regression. We develop a new task called "perpetual view generation." The goal is to create images from novel, extreme angles from a single known viewpoint. To tackle this challenge, we introduce DiffDreamer, a based-on-data approach that employs conditional diffusion models. To achieve this, we design two cross-view similarity metrics that capture both image details and 3D scene structure. We found that model performance significantly improves with the inclusion of these additional metrics. Further analysis reveals that using these metrics leads to improved training stability. Consequently, DiffDreamer produces high-quality images containing multiple scene objects that are indistinguishable from real images. Moreover, it surpasses previous generative models by generating more realistic and useful outputs. To facilitate future research, we create the PVG-Challenge dataset, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating image generation from novel angles. It comprises 8,000 scenes with 16,800 images and can be downloaded at http://diffdreamer.net. The code and models for DiffDreamer are available on http://www.nvidia.com/en-us/about-nvidia/advanced-research/. Ultimately, we found that incorporating all available data and views enhances the overall performance of the model. Specifically, we found that utilizing an AMD Radeon RX 6700 XT GPU results in superior performance and sample quality. Many interconnected systems within diverse domains exhibit dynamic, interconnected behavior, including communication networks, epidemic models, smart grids, transportation systems, and supply chains. These complex networks frequently experience unexpected disruptions, such as epidemic outbreaks or traffic accidents, which can severely exacerbate congestion, delays, or failures in other parts of the network. Consequently, it is crucial to develop a unified framework capable of forecasting, optimizing, and controlling such dynamic networks. However, this goal is complicated by two main challenges: first, accurately capturing the underlying system's dynamics using empirical data; and second, efficiently optimizing or controlling a large-scale network. This study addresses these difficulties by proposing a novel framework based on a stochastic process called the real-valued discrete time non-linear Kalman filter, real-valued continuous time linear Kalman filter, and cross-entropy algorithm. This approach incorporates a data-driven process model, optimized trajectory planning, and control law fabrication. The introduced framework's efficacy is supported by numerical simulations on a variety of dynamic epidemic models. Furthermore, we demonstrate the system's capabilities by applying it to a real-world air transport network in Europe. The study showcases the substantial potential benefits of this approach for predicting, optimizing, and controlling such dynamic networks. Specifically, it can help reduce the propagation of disruptions, such as epidemic outbreaks or traffic accidents, by leveraging data-driven optimization and control. The dynamics of a liquid layer subjected to external pressure at the interface with a fiber are investigated through simulations and experiments. Prior studies have shown that the stability of this liquid layer is influenced by the interplay between the viscous forces within the fiber and the surrounding liquid. When the liquid viscosity significantly surpasses that of the fiber, the layer remains stable. In contrast, we have found that the stability of the liquid layer can be disrupted more quickly when the liquid viscosity is lowered to be comparable to that of the fiber. In this revised scenario, the introduction of a cul-de-sac at the interface between the fiber and the liquid causes the instability to manifest more rapidly through the accumulation of defects in the liquid interface. This accelerated instability is attributed to the enhanced mass transport due to the increased liquid mobility on the fiber surface. Consequently, this revised instability is characterized as a slip-induced variant of the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. Notably, this process bears resemblance to the conventional Rayleigh-Plateau instability almost irrespective of the liquid's surface tension. The underlying mechanisms of this revised instability are comparable to those involved in the formation of Taylor cones during electrospraying. In a broader context, this study is an example of how fluid dynamics principles can unify and bridge disparate areas of research. Furthermore, this revised instability offers a potential means of electrospun fiber production, specifically through the utilization of techniques that harness convection to initiate instability. Such an approach would involve employing surface tension as a means to modulate and control the location of a capillary jet's instability. This strategy could potentially produce unique fiber textures through the deliberate introduction of surface defects during the fiber formation process. In a related vein, the interface instability offers a promising means to develop novel surface materials via the deliberate introduction of nano-particulate inclusions within a polymer matrix during the fiber production process. In this context, the introduction of nano-inclusions at specific locations within the fiber could enhance the surface-to-volume ratio of nano-particulate in the fiber, thus potentially producing nano-fiber structures with unprecedented mechanical properties. In summary, the interface instability offers significant applications in material science, specifically in the development of ultra-strong and ultra-lightweight fiber materials with controlled surface morphology at various length scales. Ultimately, the interface instability presents an opportunity to bridge the theoretical divides between electrospraying, electrospinning, surface-tension-driven instabilities, and nano-particulate-induced fiber production methods. Established techniques for scoliosis assessment using ultrasound have various drawbacks that can hinder clinical application. A novel robotic ultrasound scanning method has been introduced, promising increased reliability. We compared this new approach with traditional manual scanning in scoliosis cases by analyzing the degree of curvature and regional deformity in the lumbar spine, finding that robotic scanning yields more reliable results, with a significant decrease in measurement variability. Notably, the robotic scanning method also requires less experience, as it doesn't rely on the skill of the person operating the ultrasound. Moreover, we discovered that the curvature of the lumbar spine is consistent, making it a suitable region for scoliosis assessment using ultrasound. In conclusion, the robotic scanning method delivers more reliable spinal measurements in scoliosis cases, making it an attractive tool for clinical application. This advances the potential for ultrasound scanning to monitor spinal deformities both in the curvatures of the spine and in the shape of the deformity. Moreover, we propose that the variability in the robotic scanning method could be used in the near future to assess spinal deformity via ultrasound. Such a development would represent a significant breakthrough and open up various other clinical and research applications. Moreover, we found that the combined degree of curvature and regional deformity measures provides good characterization of scoliosis in terms of both curvature and deformity, suggesting their combined use could be a reliable and stable means of assessing scoliosis via ultrasound. Ultimately, the technology holds the promise of making ultrasound scanning a reliable tool not only for assessing existing scoliosis cases but also for detecting the condition itself. The internet's a blessing, but it's also a curse when used for cyber attacks like hate speech which harm website owners' reputation and users' mental health. Such harmful content needs to be filtered out proactively. A novel approach using feature selection methods to identify hate speech on social media is proposed in this research. Dataset collection and preprocessing involve significant challenges due to the subject nature of the data. Three feature selection techniques - Information Gain, Random Forest, and ReliefF - were tested, with the latter performing best in distinguishing hate speech from non-hate speech. A model built using selected features achieved an impressive 79.2% accuracy, 81.6% precision, and 81.5% recall. This study applies a different approach to the hate speech identification task, yielding better results with a smaller set of crucial features. Given the excessive noise in hate speech datasets, this method could aid other natural language processing tasks in similar conditions. Notably, our research surpassed the state-of-the-art performance using a substantially reduced feature set of just 11 crucial attributes. These results can benefit researchers working with imbalance datasets. Additionally, our model exhibits generalizability as it performs well on testing data, whereas the state-of-the-art model doesn't. A major outcome of this study is the creation of a new feature set which can be applied not only to hate speech detection, but also to other NLPI tasks dealing with imbalanced datasets. A related paper on hate speech dataset generation has also been published on Springer. The current experiment also makes another significant contribution by using feature selection on hate speech datasets. The proposed model along with the chosen features open up new avenues for hate speech research and can lead to other applications in NLPI. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks, composed of multiple ENCODERs and DECODERs, have shown superior performance in addressing task redundancy by sharing features efficiently. However, conventional architectures adopting standardized convolutional networks fail to account for varying data properties among task pairs, resulting in inadequate feature sharing. This drawback leads to over-reliance on two-feedforward backpropagation, which hinders the scalability of MIMO networks for task adaptation. To address these limitations, we propose MEGAOE, which introduces a customized neural component to capture diverse features. The design of this component is grounded in an in-depth analysis of class-wise feature uniqueness and commonality. Furthermore, MEGAOE incorporates a simplified decorrelation technique to promote feature sharing among task pairs. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks, including miniIMAGNET, miniCIFAR, and miniFashion, showcasing improved performance and efficiency for adaptative MIMO architectures. This research presents a comprehensive review of existing literature on analyzing historical documents by treating them as architectural problems. Specifically, we examine image datasets and tools utilized in computational research on medieval manuscripts. Our aim is to provide detailed characterizations of each dataset, facilitating easier access and understanding. These include attributes like origin, funding, standardized imaging procedures, licensing, and where available, corresponding transcriptions or translated text. Additionally, we explore features such as page, boundary, illustration, and paper segmentation characteristics, along with associated dataset repositories. By highlighting previous research accomplishments and shortcomings, we identify opportunities for further investigation. These discussions can inform future investigations and inspire new approaches within the domain of computational paleography. Ultimately, we offer suggestions and strategies for developing and utilizing datasets within the field. This research may serve as a resource for those seeking to contribute or collaborate in medieval manuscript analysis.

Over recent years, research into robotic systems has grown, with a focus on metalworking industries. Our goal in this research is to develop advanced control methods for improving the movement quality of industrial robots. The primary challenge in achieving this goal is the inherent stiffness problem associated with industrial robots, which hinders achieving smooth follow-up motions. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach based on using additional sensors to introduce more aggressive control actions. The proposed method has been tested on an KUKA SRV0300-3 robot, with results demonstrating its capacity for enhancing movement dynamics. The evaluation involved comparing the flatness-controlled robot with the standard, Intermittent Position Mode (IPM) configuration. The findings indicate that, under specific conditions, increasing the feedback rate can lead to more aggressive behavior, while maintaining accuracy. The success of this approach has also prompted further research into more advanced control methods for enhancing the movement dynamics of industrial robots. The long-term ambition is to allow operators to easily customize the movement behavior of these robots via a user-friendly interface, addressing the current lack of a transparent and adjustable solution for improving robust motion qualities. The present research represents the initial step in this direction and provides a starting point for further exploration into more sophisticated control methods for improving the movement dynamics of industrial robots. The model's ability to introduce more aggressive control actions when desired has been evaluated as a positive aspect. The proposed approach addresses a pressing issue in industrial robotics and has the potential to expand the range of applications for more aggressive control methods in this field. To comprehend the complex health trajectories of individuals, especially those who have experienced a specific event like a myocardial infarction, and to pinpoint the role of age-related factors in shaping these trajectories, it's necessary to have an appropriate statistical framework. Theoretical discussions and real-world analyses are used to demonstrate the advantages of examining multiple health states in understanding these trajectories, particularly when there are numerous states involved. A probabilistic framework, known as the multiple endpoints model, is applied to data on patients who have had a myocardial infarction to study how risk varies with age and other factors, enabling the identification of individuals who are most likely to experience future health events. A software package is used to visualize and illustrate how age impacts different health states in individuals. A simulation demonstrates how the model operates when there are varying numbers of health states involved. Finally, the capabilities of the multiple endpoints model are illustrated through a substantive analysis of how age impacts the risk of experiencing a myocardial infarction, stroke, or death in individuals who are part of a longitudinal study. A statistical test is developed to assess whether age has a non-linear impact on risk, and it's determined that age matters significantly in understanding these health trajectories. Additionally, the results show that the model's prognostic capabilities are better than those of the traditional univariate approach and that age plays a crucial role in shaping these health trajectories. The analysis also reveals that the risk of a specific health event can vary depending on the age at which it occurs, and that demographic and clinical factors, as well as social network characteristics, are all influential in understanding these myocardial infarction trajectories. A measure of life course risk is developed through a latent variable model that captures the common factors underlying different risk dimensions, and it's applied to data on patients who are at risk of experiencing a myocardial infarction. A survival analysis reveals that individuals who are at risk of a specific event can be distinguished based on the age at which it occurs by examining the strength of the latent variable, a factor that also distinguishes different kinds of health events. The results also show that the model's capabilities can be used to identify individuals who are at risk of experiencing a specific event at an early age, and that demographic and clinical factors, as well as social network characteristics, are all influential in understanding these myocardial infarction trajectories. A novel approach to data analysis reveals that the social support individuals receive from their networks can shape the trajectory of their health over time. Open boundary molecular simulations have become a crucial tool in understanding complex biological processes at interfaces. To efficiently model large systems with multiple molecules, we developed a novel integration scheme for the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. This approach simultaneously samples the electric potential at multiple molecular minima, offering several advantages over the traditional single-point method. First, it enables the efficient simulation of large systems with multiple molecules. Second, it allows the accurate representation of intramolecular charge effects without the necessity of ad-hoc parameter adjustments. Third, it offers greater control over specific electrostatic properties, all while maintaining computational performance comparable to the single-point method. We validated our approach through a series of numerical tests, examining its application to large molecules, proteins, and charged surfaces. Additionally, we analyzed the diffusion patterns of ions within various systems to gauge statistical convergence. Finally, we applied our method to model the interaction between large biomolecules and water, accurately capturing the electric structure of the resulting system. Overall, the proposed multi-center scheme represents a significant enhancement for molecular continuum modeling. It offers features previously attainable only through explicit atomistic simulations, while maintaining scalability towards large, atom-free models of biological interfaces. In any graph G, a subset of vertices R forms a k-unique set if it creates a distinct label set for all possible paths in G, requiring exactly k unique labels from a label set. A Metric Dimension problem asks for the smallest possible k-unique set. This problem has various applications across biology and physics. A generalized version, the k-unique set problem with restrictions, asks for the smallest k-unique set under specific constraints. A recent surge in research has focused on the tractability of this problem under certain restrictions. In this paper, we explore under what conditions the k-unique set problem can be efficiently solved, particularly when considering specific vertex subset parameters. A recent discovery by Boliak, Fung, Lesh, and Xu in 2017 found that the k-unique set problem can be efficiently solved for paths if parameterized by the number of subsets in R. A similar, though less efficient, solution exists for paths with two vertices. However, we propose a poly-time solution for the general Metric Dimension problem, parameterized by the number of vertices in R. A similar solution exists for series-parallel graphs, though it cannot be extended to 3-vertex-identifiable sets. However, we propose a non-recursive polynomial-time solution for the general k-unique set problem under three-vertex-identifiability, and show that the problem can be efficiently solved for bipartite graphs if parameterized by the number of vertices in R. A similar solution exists for graphs with no cycles. A long-standing conjecture suggests that the k-unique set problem can be efficiently solved for trees if parameterized by the number of subsets in R. We explore how to efficiently use the knowledge from experienced teachers to improve the learning of less experienced students. The experienced teachers provide valuable information in the form of labels or feedback, but the students struggle to fully understand this information due to its complexity and limited availability. To bridge this gap, we enhance the students' training data by incorporating additional examples that are easy for them to learn, but are also informative for the experienced teachers. To do this, we employ a new method that combines the students' ability to provide feedback with the experiences of the teachers to provide more detailed and engaging examples. The proposed approach is extensively tested through experiments on various tasks and settings, and the results show that it significantly improves the learning efficiency when compared to traditional methods that simply repeat the same examples over and over again. The improved learning efficiency is achieved through better generalization, as the students are now trained with more natural and relevant examples that are easy for them to understand. The experiments show that our method is flexible and can easily be adapted to different settings and requirements by simply adjusting the level of engagement with the experienced teachers. For K3 surfaces with an abundance of complex structure moduli, we explore the dynamics of the K\"ahler moduli. A specific region in the K\"ahler cone is identified, and within it, we construct a hyperbolic metric. As variations in the complex structure occur, this metric evolves while maintaining a particular relationship with the K\"ahler class. Ultimately, we demonstrate that one form of moduli dependence dominates, revealing that the Siegel disk of a complex multiplication K3 surface scales as the second Ray-Singer signature of its associated Shimura variety. This finding is corroborated by examining K3 surfaces derived from elliptic three-folds fiberating over specific hypergeometric curves, as well as those associated with the family of van Hoecke--Graaf K3 surfaces. Meanwhile, calculating the Siegel disk for the primary node of a quiver connects it to Yau--Tian--Yau's formulation of K\"ahler--Calabi--Yau theory. Consequently, through an extensive analysis, we establish a moduli-dependent relationship between the Siegel disk and the K\"ahler--Calabi--Yau obstruction, quantified by the $c_1(-T)^{\otimes 2}$. Our findings are further extended to include higher-dimensional fibrations, specifically those attending to the Birkhoff--Wolf orbit of an element in a Siegel disk. Interestingly, upon exploring the intersection of this text with recent findings of van Hoecke--Graaf K3 surface families, we discover a geometrically equivalent, albeit limited, generalization. Therefore, to avoid unnecessary complications, we choose to abandon further investigations of this higher-dimensional problem. Throughout this work, we adopt a relatively straightforward approach to verifying the hyperbolicity of our constructed metrics. Nonetheless, supporting supplementary evidence for these claims can be found in an accompanying research notice of the first listed author, dated 2021. A stochastic Newton method in a distributed setting is proposed to solve a broad class of convex optimization problems, specifically quadratic programs and its extension, strongly convex programs. By utilizing extra computational resources, called agents, the problem is broken down and solved separately at each iteration. At each step, the method is executed in two phases: estimation and optimization. First, individual agents estimate the gradient of the objective function, then they update their local solutions using Newton-based calculations. To ensure convergence within a predetermined margin of error, the method employs a technique called double sampling. As the method runs, the error margin decreases with the inverse of the iteration number, the square root of the number of iterations, the square root of the number of agents, and the inverse of the sampling rate. Numerical tests validate the method's efficiency, especially when the sampling rate is optimized. Moreover, the results indicate that the method outperforms existing methods, including a centralized Newton method, a distributed gradient method, and a distributed Newton method that does not utilize double sampling. A substantial speedup is observed when the method is executed in a multi-agent setting, especially when the number of agents exceeds the square root of the iteration number. Investigating the properties of the generalized Gaussian process leads to considering manifolds of generalized Gaussian random fields as manifolds with sections that satisfy the lower bound of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. In this context, the topological structure of the space includes minimal smooth structures, enabling the identification of a Riemannian metric that makes the space an infinite-dimensional manifold. A random field map is then analyzed to determine if it is smooth, and if so, to find its differential. Moreover, the shortest paths between field values are explored and conditions are derived to determine if they exist. Finally, the stochastic dynamics of a particle moving along the shortest paths are derived and used to develop a test for determining whether the particle moves more freely or less freely. A practical test has been proposed for this purpose. Moreover, the space of generalized Gaussian processes can be redefined based on this analysis, and the redefinition has significant implications for the space when it contains at least three field values. In specific cases, when the field values come from a Gaussian distribution with a non-zero and finite variance, the space can be redefined without such implications. In systems that rely on Named Entity Retrieval (NER), vast collections of entity data are readily accessible, requiring precise entity selection to provide relevant context. Unlike conventional tasks, our work focuses on developing a suitable context from the entire pool of entities, rather than pre-qualifying it. To achieve this, our proposed method, Term Relevance Response (TER), determines the most relevant context by considering each entity's relevance in relation to the search query. Unlike existing entity retrieval methods that employ pre-defined contexts or nearest neighbor approaches with fixed depth, our dynamic entity retrieval approach, TER, automatically determines the most relevant context by dynamically adjusting the number of nearest entities (K) and considering all entities as reference points. We introduce a new search dataset called CRED, containing 38k English search queries and their respective entities. We evaluate our method through both theoretical and experimental analyses on the CRED dataset. The results reveal the significant impact of incorporating more entities and the proposed adaptive entity retrieval approach, outperforming a competitor method with a 19.1% average improvement in F1 score. Understanding software requirements involves both a broad perspective and in-depth analysis. While many approaches aim to increase understanding by examining requirements from multiple professional viewpoints, overlooking the importance of technical documentation in understanding software requirements leaves a significant gap in the current knowledge base. This document offers a fresh outlook, by instead focusing on utilizing technical documentation as a primary information source. Consequently, a novel method has been developed that analyzes text from manuals, guides, and similar sources to extract detailed specifications from software projects involving object-oriented technologies. The resulting extracted data can then be visualized using class and sequence diagrams to facilitate easy comprehension by developers and users. The proposed method was evaluated through two experiments: one examining its applicability as a cross-project analysis tool and another comparing its results to manually extracted specifications from a individual project. The evaluation confirmed the method's effectiveness, demonstrating that it surpasses a leading requirement understanding approach by 25% in terms of accuracy. With the capacity for improved cross-project analysis and high within-project effectiveness, this work views technical documentation as a vital component of the requirements extraction landscape. The method's source code has been made publicly available for further development and improvement. The code can be accessed via https://github.com/getting-contribs/digdes. Our research introduces a unique technique, the blend generative adversarial network (BGAN), which combines the advantages of generative adversarial networks and blend models to protect against these attacks. The blend model, which treats the input as a combination of two separate inputs, is paired with a generative adversarial network to improve resistance to adversarial examples. Our BGAN model consists of an encoder, blend network, classifier, and generator, which work together to produce a blend that resembles legitimate data and an adversarial instance that is indistinguishable from the blend. By training the BGAN in a semi-synthetic environment with semi-evasion attacks, we achieve a significant improvement in resistance to adversarial examples. Moreover, the extracted features from the semi-evasion attacks demonstrate superior performance compared to those obtained through traditional training methods, while requiring fewer support examples. Ultimately, our proposed BGAN exhibits a 10% or more improvement in 10-fold cross-validation accuracy compared to a high-performance deep learning model with similar architecture and parameters. Therefore, our BGAN serves as a reliable solution for real-world modal classification tasks. The source code and executables for our paper can be found at https://github.com/muhariff/blend-GAN. We've developed a universal approach that utilizes learning techniques to identify and correct errors in dynamical system models. Although models often contain flaws, direct identification of these issues via observation data is usually not feasible. However, detecting model mistakes (miscalculations that occur during numerical integration within the model) is possible, either by using external information (e.g. ground truth) or by analyzing numerical results without intervention (e.g. comparing outcomes with model behavior). Our method employs a two-step process: Firstly, we design a neural network to analyze and detect model mistakes. A popular theory among cosmologists suggests that a significant portion of dark matter in the universe could be composed of primordial black holes (PBHs).  Quantifying the quantity of PBHs capable of constituting 100% of dark matter requires a thorough comprehension of three elements: (1) the mass of PBHs, (2) the density of matter within these PBHs, and (3) the density of dark matter in the universe.  A web-based calculator called PopSyCLE was created to facilitate this calculation, which also produces supplementary graphs as an added benefit.  In the calculator's core, three key functions are offered: (a) the calculation of a primordial black hole's mass based on its initial density and the density of dark matter in the universe, (b) the determination of a PBH's matter density based on its mass and the density of dark matter in the universe, as well as (c) the calculation of a PBH's mass that would yield a 50% matter, 50% dark matter composition.  Additionally, the web-based calculator includes functions for generating (1) a graph illustrating how mass and the matter density of PBHs are related, (2) a graph illustrating how mass and the matter-to-dark matter ratio are related and (3) a graph illustrating how mass and the dark matter content of PBHs are related.  Below is the link to access the web-based calculator: https://santosetc.github.io/PopSyCLE/ (verified March 2022).  In the full paper, the underlying source code of the web-based calculator is provided.  Also included in the full paper are the Doxygen-generated documentation of the web-based calculator and the relevant Commits from the GitHub repository where the web-based calculator was developed.  A recent study provided upper limits on non-thermalized PBHs that have a mass of less than the mass of the sun.  Since our calculator was developed prior to the publication of the study, the results obtained using the calculator may not be entirely consistent with the study's conclusions.  Ultimately, the study led to the update of the relevant lower limits on the mass of PBHs capable of constituting 100% of dark matter in the universe, with mass values ranging from approximately 5.16 geV to 3.55 zeV, with the exclusion of mass values that would lead to matter densities that are not feasible for known astrophysical objects. By analyzing these simulations, we identify unique phases that exhibit ordered and disordered states. Specifically, we find that the ordered states exhibit uniform and modulated splay orientations, while the disordered state behaves like a gas-liquid mixture. Furthermore, we discover compact and expanded hexagonal column phases with multiple layers, as well as hexagonal columns with loose surrounding particles. LSTM-based language models have been widely used in various NLP tasks but
often suffer from massive parameters, leading to high computation costs.
One potential solution is adjusting the existing model with a smaller set of
parameters to improve performance in specific downstream tasks without
retraining the entire model, thus improving efficiency. This paper explores
different adjustment methods to enhance the performance of an LSTM model in
three specific NLP tasks: sentence classification, question answering, and
text classification. The experiments compare the effectiveness of an adaptation
method that updates the token embeddings with a more relevant meaning, while
using fixed word embeddings, to other adjustment techniques. The results show
that our approach successfully reduces computational costs and boosts model
performance in all three tasks without requiring full model retraining. On
average, the proposed method achieves a 6.8% increase in F1 score, a 4.7% drop
in parameter count, and a 37x speedup in training time relative to the best
baseline. Moreover, when evaluated on the SQuAD task, the same adapted model
reaches an F1 score of 88.6, outperforming the top-pruned model by 0.9%. This
success highlights the potential of adjusting pre-trained language models to
boost both performance and efficiency in specific downstream tasks through
special token adaptation. This research also makes available a public GitHub
repository containing our code, data, and experimental results. This study has
been presented at the IJCA'22 conference. Furthermore, a related study is
available on the NEURLINKS'22 workshop.

Preference ranking systems are built on a non-contextual preference model where every pair of items has a well-defined preference order. This paper delves into an enhanced context-aware approach where preference orders depend on specific situations. We propose a new algorithm for setting up context-based preference orders and demonstrate its capabilities in resolving the set addition problem, which involves finding the best subset of items given certain requirements. Unlike conventional methods, our algorithm excels in handling large datasets and provides superior results compared to other techniques. Moreover, our algorithm's output can be interpreted as a single, unified preference order, unlike other methods that often report multiple solutions. We illustrate the value of our algorithm's output through two real-world applications one from a travel-related domain and another from the domain of data reduction. Although our algorithm's output may lack the precision required for making highly specific preference judgments, it still captures important information that can aid in making informed domain-level design choices. We highlight the significance of these contributions and provide a vision for their future development. Our algorithm's output can be accessed through our public GitHub repository. Finally, all of our algorithm's code has been made open-source and can be directly executed from our repository without any further modifications. This repository uses the Python programming language and relies on a few other open-source libraries, in particular the scio library for data manipulation and analysis. We expect our future research to utilize Python as well, given its growing popularity in the AI community as a language for AI research. We also briefly discuss how our algorithm could be used as a tool for teaching various AI-related concepts to students. We plan to further enhance our algorithm as described in the conclusion section. Our algorithm was presented at the IBAI2020 conference under the name "Contextual vs Non-Contextual Set Addition for Information Retrieval". Our algorithm received the best paper award at the IBAI2020 conference. Our repository was last updated on July 26, 2021. Our algorithm's Python implementation was significantly improved by the scio library, which provides a lot of useful data manipulation and analysis functionality. Our algorithm was suggested by Dr. S. K. Mishra, a renowned Indian Professor from the Bhubaneswar city. Our algorithm's testing was carried out on computational machines manufactured by Dell and Lenovo, which are reputable companies based in the USA and China, respectively. Our algorithm's development was motivated by the real-world domains of travel and reduction. Our algorithm was presented at the IBAI2020 conference under the area of Natural Language Processing (NLP).

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that entropy, internal energy, and configurational entropy are interconnected in a specific manner, which is influenced by temperature, volume, and the strength of interactions. This relationship allows for the calculation of heat capacities and coefficients regulating volume changes due to temperature variations. By analyzing these factors, we can determine whether a given polymer fluid undergoes glassification, and we have identified criteria that distinguish two types of lattice cluster parameters based on their behavior at zero temperature. Our analysis reveals that the strength of interactions rather than the state of ordering within the fluid affects its tendency to form glasses. At high temperatures, above the liquid's characteristic cooling point, the polymer's internal energy and entropy behave similarly, enabling an almost perfect alignment between entropy and internal energy or the entropy's excess and energy's excess. When cooled through this characteristic temperature, the polymer's internal energy and entropy start to diverge, becoming increasingly disconnected as it approaches the glass transition. Upon further cooling, the polymer's internal energy develops a deeper minimum at zero temperature, while its entropy continues to increase due to increasing restrictions, resulting in a positive jump. Conversely, the volume of the polymer displays a negative jump at the glass transition, resulting in a negative coefficient regulating volume changes due to temperature variations. Our findings are compared to simulations of di-ethyl-amino-benzene and oligomerized ethylene, supporting our theoretical conclusions. These conclusions are further broadened to cover mixtures of non-polymeric components and pure fluids. It is predicted that the divergence of the polymer's internal energy and entropy can be observed not only during cooling but also by increasing the strength of interactions at high temperatures. Previous studies on transformer-based language models have consistently shown a
tendency to reject irregular sentences and maintain accuracy in parsing
correct sentences. To explore this tendency further, we treat language models
as if they were being "socialized" and develop a method to measure and evaluate
their capacity for accepting and adapting to new information during this process.
We create a series of tasks where models can adjust to sentence modifications
without violating grammatical rules, and discover that some models exhibit a
behavior similar to "suspension of judgment" when encountering unfamiliar
sentences. We found that large language models like BART and T5 tend to process
irregular sentences in a manner related to psychological defenses, specifically
as a form of repression, where the models may deny or refuse information that
contradicts existing beliefs. On the other hand, models like RoBERTa appear to
process such sentences through a form of identification, where the models may
internalize and incorporate new information without difficulty. Ultimately, we
found that large language models, regardless of size or type, can effectively
process and accept new information over time with continuous socialization.
Our findings suggest that socialization can effectively improve the capacity of
large language models to comprehend and generate text. We think that further
investigation into the potential connections between a model's "rejection
behavior" and its overall performance in language understanding and generation
tasks could be a highly profitable area of study. Our dataset and code are
publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/AllanLin94/rejection-socialization. We hope that this research will serve as a foundation for exploring the potential connections between a model's "rejection behavior" and its language abilities. In neural machine translation, the lack of a future perspective hinders its translation quality. Focus, which allocates computational resources to specific input words, can be manipulated to enhance translation relevance. By integrating Focus with a lookahead feature that considers future inputs, the model can prioritize crucial words during decoding. We demonstrate that by regulating Focus, the model can be coerced into translating responsibly, effectively utilising the lookahead feature to improve its translation accuracy. We successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed method on two sets of challenging translation tasks: one involving inaccurate translations with high saliency and another involving noisy input translations. The method's superiority was established through both objective and human evaluations on the IWSLT and WMT datasets. Our project code is openly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/lafg-nmt. Additionally, Asharakeh et al. (2021) provide an analogous method for neural machine translation, which does not incorporate the Focus mechanism. While the methods differ, they share a common goal of leveraging the lookahead feature to boost translation accuracy. The method's superiority was demonstrated through both objective and human evaluations on the IWSLT dataset. Our project code is openly available at https://github.com/multinat/exploiting-the-future. The method described in Liang et al. (2020) also does not involve the Focus mechanism and instead makes controlled decisions using the attention distribution to engage or disengage the attention module for specific words during training. It was proven that the method enhances the translation quality on the WMT 2006 Russian-to-English dataset through both objective evaluations. Our project code is openly available at https://github.com/mutsupachin/pseudo-tag. The method presented in Wang et al. (2019) also does not incorporate the Focus mechanism and instead makes controlled decisions using the FutureC reward to balance the translation accuracy between various evaluation metrics. It was proven that the method enhances the translation quality on the WMT 2019 Devenish Russian-to-English dataset through both objective evaluations. Our project code is openly available at https://github.com/sgwang19/future-nmt. The method described in Zhao et al. (2019) also does not involve the Focus mechanism and instead makes controlled decisions using the FutureC reward to engage an additional decoder for fine-tuning on the NIST metrics on the English-to-Chinese translation task. It was proven that the method enhances the translation quality on the NIST dataset through both human evaluations. Our project code is openly available

Papadopoulos and Temzelides published a paper in 2021, proposing a framework for valuing Asian options based on the characteristics of Markov processes. This note highlights significant flaws in their main argument regarding the connection between Markov processes and pricing methods for geometric and arithmetic Asian options. Specifically, authors point out that the mentioned relationship only holds when a state space is compact. Consequently, many Markov processes do not satisfy this condition. For instance, diffusions with infinite state spaces, which include popular models like the Black-Scholes geodesic and the non-speculative fractional Brownian motion, cannot be represented as homeomorphisms. Furthermore, in these cases, the value of an Asian option may exceed the price of a standard European option, leading to option values that are unbounded from above for fixed strike prices. The possibility of unbounded values for option values from below is also considered. These issues render the pricing method in question unreliable, as it yields incorrect results for certain Markov processes. To address these shortfalls, authors provide an alternative explanation for the relationship between the discounted expected payoff of an arithmetic Asian option and the sum of the discounted expected values of the processes at any time. Then, they suggest a universal pricing formula for arithmetic Asian options based on the concept of projective spaces. This formula is verified to be correct and efficient in its ability to produce a unique numerical value with every Markov process, state space, and strike price input. The new approach outperforms the original method as it provides bounded option values independently of the state space and strike prices. The outperforming result holds for both geometric and arithmetic options. The new concept is evaluated in terms of its computational and informational requirements. The study also examines the potential for further research related to the bounding property of the projective space approach. As an implementation of the new concept, authors provide a detailed numerical solution for a non-speculative fractional Brownian geometric Asian option using a finite mesh approach. The study concludes by considering the potential for further research related to the pricing and bounding methods for Asian options. Specifically, the new concept could be applied to evaluate multi-asset options, which are difficult to value using traditional methods. Moreover, the pricing approach holds promise for use in modeling real estate values. The universe's gamma-ray emission is primarily produced by hadronic interactions between high-speed charged particles and thermal electrons in galaxy clusters. The limited gamma-ray signal from these clusters is due to a massive, diffuse gas distribution. The question remains about the origin of the charged particles responsible for this signal. This paper presents a theoretical model where cosmic rays originate from interactions with photons within dark matter halos that exceed the cosmic background's intensity. The model accounts for the gamma-ray signal observed in galaxy clusters and sets constraints on the level of dark matter halo photon intensity above the cosmic background. The model also has implications for the cosmic evolution of hadronic components and the radiation emitted, though the current research finds this path unlikely given existing data. An alternative explanation for the gamma-ray signal from galaxy clusters involves the halos themselves. The observed gamma-ray signal in clusters like Perseus and Coma can be matched by charged particles produced at the clusters' edges. The observed signal is decreased due to diffuse clusters' photon field dispersing the high-energy charged particles throughout the clusters. The frequency of highly intense photon fields influences the spatial and energy distribution of the cosmic rays within clusters. The relationship between photon field intensity and cosmic ray intensity in clusters and its impact on the gamma-ray energy spectrum is also discussed. The model predicts near-IR radiation in galaxy clusters to be decreased due to a dispersive effect from lower-intensity photon fields in their ICM. The effect on the CRs in clusters with lower ICM photon field intensity is less significant, which also influences the CRs' beta-ratio. The effect on clusters with cool plasmas is more complex, involving synchrotron radiation from particles generated by active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity. The effect on clusters with shock waves is also significant at lower z clusters due to dispersion. The effect on clusters with magnetic fields is also significant; however, its impact on radiation is minimal. Observations of magnetic fields in clusters with star formation reveal the potential for the cosmic rays originating from dark matter halos containing intense photons. High-resolution, long-term observations of the ICM and star formation clusters are required to confirm the effect of photon field dispersion on the gamma-ray signal and charged particles in galaxy clusters. The effect's verification will also allow for the use of gamma-ray astronomy to determine the photon field intensity within galaxy cluster halos. The effect's implications are also present in hadronic processes at higher energy levels, which is consistent with the starburst galaxy data. The effect's lower-energy counterpart has also been observed

By building on this revised framework, we explore improved analytical methods for calculating particle creation and apply these to a freshly identified area of study. In an inflationary model where the universe's symmetry is unbroken but exhibits anomalies, a novel mechanism allows for single graviton emission, despite a massive mass gap. This results in an unique feature in cosmic microwave background spectra. Understanding how visual concepts are represented within Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) is crucial for creating transparent and robust visual learning systems. By exploring DCNN representations, researchers can address a range of important questions regarding the mechanisms underlying generalization, biases, and potential biases in DCNNs. Unfortunately, the current methods for measuring feature representations in DCNs are often restricted to simplified scenarios or they fail to offer useful insights into the workings of large DCNNs. This research introduces a novel framework that employs a global image embedding to direct layer-specific feature filter focus. This novel filter focus can be easily extracted from pre-trained DCNNs and provides a highly interpretable visualization of visual concepts across different levels of a network. Furthermore, the extracted filter focus is capable of modeling a range of semantic concept relationships. The results demonstrate that the proposed filter focus enables a more accurate assessment of feature representation and provides a novel way to visualize and compare the underlying concepts within class activation maps. Ultimately, the extracted filter focus offers significant insights into the representations and structures learned by DCNNs, enabling a deeper understanding of visual generalization by humans and machines. The developed tool enables a thorough and novel exploration of visual biases found in DCNNs and can also uncover implicit biases and assumptions that have not been previously reported in the literature. Ultimately, the proposed DCNN visualizations provide a means for addressing and reducing unwanted biases in visual AI models. This paper adapts the recently-devised Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture to a Question-Answering (QA) task, retrieving relevant context passages based on a given question and then employing a generator model to produce an answer. We refine the entire RAG architecture, comprising both the context retriever and the generator model, to overcome limitations in contemporary QA solutions. This work refines the RAG architecture to attain a new state-of-the-art performance on the WikiQA dataset, surpassing the then-state-of-the-art performance on the TriviaQA dataset, and also achieving superior results on the FactVista dataset. We successfully address context missing issues by fine-tuning the entire RAG architecture to produce more complete answers. This study focuses on the asymptotic analysis of polynomials orthogonal to a specific function, defined by $\frac{1}{NH(r)\ln(NH(r))}$, where $N$ is the polynomial degree, $H(r)$ is an entropy function, and $r$ represents the distance from the complex unit circle in the Schur C-domain. We investigate the coefficients and recurrence coefficients of these polynomials and derive the asymptotic forms for their zeros under two different entropy conditions. Furthermore, to verify our theoretical results, an error estimate for the zero location of these polynomials is also derived. We observe that these polynomials exhibit unique characteristics, including near-zero and wide spectral gaps in their asymptotic forms, which can be attributed to the presence of logarithmic influences. This behavior is reminiscent of strongly orthogonal polynomials with a logarithmic factor in their defining influence function, as discussed in the book by Simon. We also note that these polynomials are part of a larger class of meromorphic functions under a specific condition on $r$. Finally, to facilitate numerical computations for the entropy function, an algorithm is presented. Numerical examples are provided to support our theoretical findings. As an application of these results, we investigate the asymptotic forms for the zeros of polynomials under a specific logarithmic weight $r^2\ln^2(r)$, which is known to be strongly orthogonal. However, the logarithmic influence is a key factor in this case, as the entropy function diverges as $r$ approaches 1 from the right, limiting the degree of the polynomials. This behavior is in sharp contrast to strongly orthogonal polynomials under other weights for real and complex variables. We observe that these polynomials exhibit distinct, nonring behaviors, including nonclosed geometric configurations for their zeros. This behavior is also reflected in their recurrence coefficients. Consequently, their asymptotic analysis under a logarithmic weight is a critical and distinctive case. To this end, we first analyze the recurrence coefficients of these polynomials by deriving the asymptotic forms for the coefficients of the three-term recurrence relation using a differential equation approach for orthogonal polynomials. We also investigate the algebraic and geometric properties of these polynomials, including their zeros and the interior of their spectral gaps using a numerical approach. Numerical examples are provided to support our theoretical findings and confirm the uniqueness of their asymptotic analysis under a logarithmic weight. Online crowdsourcing platforms, such as MTurk, allow researchers to assess user interactions and gather data, but doing so is complicated by the presence of uncooperative and unqualified workers. In this study, we investigate the process of engaging qualified MTurk workers through a multi-ringed target-style approach. We first circle around and evaluate existing studies on this topic, then design, test and report on a new method that utilizes target-style evaluation rings to identify and select top MTurk workers. Our study shows that by focusing on workers who hit inner rings of previous tasks, we can recruit top MTurk workers who consistently produce high-quality work across a range of tasks, even when they don't consistently perform well in all experiments. Moreover, our strategy allows us to engage and pay top workers significantly less than would be required by recruiting unqualified workers. In the end, we offer strategies for effectively hiring the best MTurk workers and engaging them at a low cost. Our MTurk hiring strategy has far-reaching implications that extend to other labor markets as well. Our code for this research is freely shared on a GitHub repository. However, with the establishment of the Large Hadron Collider, there is now a more nuanced understanding that enables the re-examination of taste-changing neutral currents. This updated study investigates taste-changing neutral currents in the context of top-t pair production, a process with significant luminosity accumulation at the LHC. Two main scenarios are explored: one involving next-to-leading order taste-changing neutral current contributions to top-t pair production at next-to-leading order, and another requiring an estimation of its size via a postdictive analysis based on next-to-leading order top-quark decay properties. The study finds that taste-changing neutral currents could potentially make up a notable fraction of top-t pair production, with a sizeable one being on the order of 10% or larger. Moreover, it appears that while next-to-leading order taste-changing neutral current contributions are feasible, their exact magnitude remains constrained due to complex calculational difficulties. As a result, a postdictive analysis seems to be the more reliable approach for understanding the role of taste-changing neutral currents in top-t pair production. Ultimately, this analysis concludes with potential constraints on complete electroweak unification due to several parameters in top-quark decay properties. Notably, it appears that taste-changing neutral currents can potentially allow for larger values of the SU(2)L SU(2) doublet Higgs mass, a capability not observed in earlier studies. This framework differentiates Augmented Synthetic Intelligence by incorporating external intelligence sources. These supplementary intelligent entities can supply data, share expertise, and communicate with each other through collective learning mechanisms. We contend that this hybrid approach overcomes the limitations of standalone Synthetic Intelligence and paves the way for more sophisticated intelligence. In this study, we will examine the potential benefits and drawbacks of Augmented Synthetic Intelligence. By exploring this concept further, we may uncover new avenues for advancements beyond traditional Synthetic Intelligence formulations.
