Approximation techniques leveraging Gaussian Processes have proliferated throughout the scientific community in recent years. While the numerous kernels developed thus far have been primarily empirically constructed or tailored to specific problems, a novel approach involves breaking down these kernels into simpler component forms. This work introduces a comprehensive library of basic approximation expressions, from which a range of Gaussian Process kernels can be derived. Furthermore, we present an algorithm that recovers these fundamental expressions from the underlying Gaussian Process kernels. The main advantages of this method are (1) a unifying framework that simplifies kernel comparison and development; (2) the ability to apply initial domain knowledge to craft a suitable approximation expression, thereby reducing the complexity of Gaussian Process optimization, and (3) the possibility of combining and modifying existing expressions to address problems that have thus far been neglected. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through its successful reconstruction of various kernels, as well as its application to the steering control of an autonomous car. This interaction can give rise to a boundary-winding Pauli obstruction that impedes the formation of a robust, topologically protected state. A state of this type is known as a topological phase of Bose-Einstein condensation and is characterized by unique topological features in both its bulk and boundary. A phenomenon of this kind was observed in a recent experiment conducted on a superconducting circuit. Here, we describe the theoretical underpinnings that led to this groundbreaking observation and other predictions that may arise from it. Notably, the emergence of this type of obstruction is a prime example of how a hidden topological structure can manifest in a broad class of weakly interactive quantum systems through symmetry spontaneous breaking. Moreover, the anisotropy introduced by the obstruction may give rise to a unique disorder in space that is lacking in both bulk and boundary, causing a unique rounding effect in the transition. This phenomenon is reminiscent of the rounding effect typically seen in 2D systems but is instead applied to a 1D system. Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for rapid feedback and initial assessment of code functionality. However, test code, like any other code, can become flawed over time, possibly due to inadequate maintenance or transformation during refactoring operations. The presence of test smells within test suites can cause tests to malfunctions, producing incorrect results, like compilation errors or failed executions. From a software developers standpoint, researchers aimed to understand the frequency, causes, and perceived impact of test smells, rather than a purely metric-based approach. A two-part empirical study was conducted: Firstly, developers were asked to identify 175 test methods suspected to contain test smells, and secondly, they were asked to provide details on either the cause of the smell or the consequences it had on the behavior of the test methods. From the 94 responses collected, researchers learned that 61% of test smells were categorized as basic (e.g. simple assertion with expected result), totaling 53 test methods. Furthermore, developers stated that 53% of test smells produced no errors at all, while 20% failed to run successfully, leading to questions about the effectiveness of failing tests. The study also revealed that 49% of test smells were produced during refactoring operations, suggesting that this process may be the primary cause of test smells. The study's findings provide valuable insights into the challenges software developers encounter, supporting the daily work of maintainers of open-source software projects. Ultimately, researchers were able to gather a comprehensive understanding of test smells, working towards developing strategies to minimize their occurrence during refactoring operations. The study's data can be accessed at https://github.com/stefanobuzza/empirical-su. A practical follow-up intervention involving the maintenance of the Z3 open-source project confirmed that implementing failing tests has a positive effect on the quality of the test code. Frequent commits tend to correlate with a negative impact on test quality, indicating a future research opportunity. A practical assessment of how tech companies like Microsoft implement the described intervention can be conducted, providing first-hand knowledge of this policy's effectiveness in industry environments. Moreover, Microsoft's policy could serve as a source of inspiration for other open-source communities to adopt similar changes. We have developed the multi-photon event generator, KKMCee, designed for simulating electron-positron pair creation and lepton and quark pair production in colliders through photon-mediated interactions. The generator utilizes the known Born cross sections supplemented by the NNLO level corrections to ensure high accuracy, specifically up to the NLO level for stability in the high energy range. The KKMCee generator includes multiple photon-ee, $\gamma\gamma$, and qq creation processes, making it a versatile tool for colliders operating at various energy levels. Furthermore, this event generator is not only optimized for electron-positron colliders but can also be applied to proton-electron and future electron-proton colliders. Ultimately, the KKMCee events can be used to analyze a broad range of phenomena within the standard model and its theoretical frameworks. The generator is now freely available online at the MCCINC @KITLIIS website. A detailed, graphical explanation of the event selection process can be found at the interactive MCCINC explanation @WIZDOM website. In this paper, several event simulation results are presented to evaluate the accuracy of the KKMCee events, specifically across a range of colliders operating at varying energy levels. The investigation reveals that the major discrepancies between the NNLO events and the Monte Carlo events from KKMCee are less than 1% for most of the tested colliders. The largest discrepancies, approximately at the order of 0.2%, occur at the LHeC and the future electron-proton colliders. It is worth noting that the generator not only generates accurate statistics for colliders operating at high energy levels but also successfully replicates experimental data with negligible residual systematic errors. To tackle the escalating computational demands of large-scale tensors, a time-efficient, randomized approach to approximating any component of an SVD for a 3D tensor using an adaptable number of passes is developed, where each pass involves matrix operations that can be performed in O(N^2 n) operations and is subsequently proven to converge to the exact tensor SVD in O(log^2 n) passes. Implementing the approach in a manner that leverages ongoing computations enables it to scale efficiently even for very large tensors. In situations where resources are limited, the approach allows for an accurate estimation of the 2nd and 3rd mode singular values in essentially O(log^2 n) passes. Furthermore, the approach is applied to a real-world problem, specifically processing a full volume of cardiac MR images totaling 6 GB and successfully reconstructing the SVD in under 2 minutes with an accurate margin of 1% on a 2017 MacBook Pro. In addition, the approach is evaluated against a recently developed, 2D method that was specifically optimized for efficiency and is compared against a vectorized, 3D method that is computationally intensive but provides exact tensor SVD. Results show that in most cases, the randomized approach is 2-3 times faster than the more efficient method, indicating that it is a valuable tool for scalable tensor processing. Lastly, the approach is compared against an existing, randomized method that is specifically tailored for 3D tensors but is inherently more pass-hungry than the developed technique before converging to the exact SVD. In this comparison, the approach is shown to be faster by at least an order of magnitude in terms of passes required to achieve the same level of accuracy. Overall, the developed technique is an efficient solution for processing scalable tensors by dynamically adapting to computational resources and is a valuable tool for extracting valuable quantitative information from 3D images. As such, the code has been made open-source and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/kevinwong-uncCsi. Utilizing this same framework, the approach can be extended to handle even more complex dimensions in 4D, 5D images by adding an extra pass at the end, resulting in a total of at most log^3 m passes. A detailed breakdown of this expansion and the new method's efficiency has been described in a follow-up paper. The developed technique is an efficient solution for processing scalable tensors by adapting to computational resources and is particularly useful for extracting valuable quantitative information from 3D images. In various real-world applications, dynamic networks are encountered, which necessitate graph embedding techniques that incorporate temporal information to capture patterns and relationships. This demand has led to the development of several methods addressing evolving graphs with changes in nodes, edges, community structure, and centrality over time. These approaches, known as spatio-temporal embeddings, have extensive applications in tasks such as search engines, drug engineering, and social media analysis. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the most advanced methodologies in this area, categorizing them by the type of temporal information they handle. Additionally, the challenges in this field are discussed, followed by a presentation of future research directions and promising avenues for exploration. This survey aims to offer readers a clear understanding of the state of the art and guidance on the design of novel spatio-temporal embedding techniques. [article:2021.0128464]

Recently, a highly accurate ground-state electron density map was published for the $^7$H nucleus. This $^7$H is a loosely bound system with a small binding energy of about 0.81 MeV and a corresponding neutron separation width of around 17 fm. Given the significant distance between the protons and neutrons within the $^7$H system, it is reasonable to view it as an excitation of $^3$H with four neutrons. We propose that the $^7$H ground state can be treated as an excited state of $^3$H and four neutrons, where each neutron has an average position. This is inspired by the work of Friedman and Lee in $^4$He. This view provides a simple explanation for the significant size of the $^7$H system and is in line with the recently-published ground-state electron density map. This scenario suggests a distinct spatial structure within the $^7$H system, where different regions contain either three neutrons or all four neutrons. This is in agreement with calculations from Faddeev equations, which demonstrate a significant difference between systems with three or four neutrons. This is in contrast to the situation in $^6$He, where two neutrons can move freely within the bound system. These differences between $^7$H and $^6$He can be attributed to the presence of an additional neutron in the former, leading to increased size and a lower density within the bound system. This is because when one neutron moves away from the core, more space is created and this tends to expand the system. Conversely, in $^6$He, the size and density are determined by the two moving neutrons, which does not change significantly with position. This is in line with the system's negative parity and is attributed to the presence of a single moving neutron in the two-neutron s-wave pair. These findings highlight the utility of the $^7$H system as an excitation of $^3$H with four neutrons and suggest the potential for further investigations into other 2S, 1p and 1d states within the neutron-rich $^7$H system. In many countries, including England, contact tracing for COVID-19 has been a complex challenge. To aid in this effort, numerous private companies and data-driven startups offered their services, but also posed significant data protection and privacy risks. To mitigate these concerns, some organizations, such as DSGMC and others in this study, formed local tracing partnerships based on existing data assets. This research examines the value of these partnerships in supporting contact tracing in various areas of England. To conduct this study, we identified four local tracing partnerships that utilized existing data sources to contribute to the national contact tracing effort. By quantifying their contributions, we demonstrated that the partnership leveraging insurance data helped identify nearly 340,000 people, while those using supermarket loyalty data and fitness tracker data identified around 220,000 and 90,000 individuals respectively. Additionally, we discovered that the young adult age group (20-30) was over-represented in the fitness tracker data, but under-rerepresented in the supermarket loyalty data. The findings of this study highlight the significance of local tracing partnerships in augmenting national contact tracing efforts. They also suggest the potential for prioritizing specific age groups and socioeconomic demographics when designing local tracing campaigns. Ultimately, this research emphasizes the importance of leveraging existing data assets to inform and optimize COVID-19 contact tracing efforts. The analysis presented here is indicative of a broader set of applications where machine learning and data analysis can be applied to reveal new insights into individuals' behavior. Such research may yield valuable insights if conducted responsibly and with a focus on enhancing societal efforts during data-poor pandemics. The existing method described in this paper could be extended to accommodate more complex scenarios where multiple local tracing campaigns are conducted in parallel. Melotte 72 is a tightly packed, young open star cluster located near the Sun with minimal interference from background noise due to its small diameter of approximately 15 minutes in radius on the celestial map. Located approximately 2,300 parsecs away from Earth, it is characterized by its relatively narrow diameter and age of about 68 million years. This study relies on Gaia DR2's precise satellite-based distance measurements to examine the cluster's structural features. Calculations of fundamental parameters, including the cluster's central density, total mass, and radial density distribution, were conducted using standardized statistical methods. Notably, our findings show that Melotte 72's total mass is increasing at a rate of 0.19 solar masses per year, a trend potentially attributed to two possible explanations - the presence of a pre-main-sequence wind or an ongoing star formation episode. We also determined the cluster's structural features using Sersic fit and radial density profiles, revealing a distorted isodensity half-radius on the north-south axis with a 1.39 sigma discrepancy from circular shape symmetry. This study suggests Melotte 72 is characterized by a suspect mass distribution within its core and possibly asymmetric, non-circular in shape, with further discussion of these findings provided. Melotte 72 is one of a few young star clusters near the Sun with Gaia DR2's satellite-based distance measurements, making this study valuable in understanding basic physical properties of the cluster as well as its structural features. This study contributes to the development of melotte 72's dynamical characteristics models. This research offers an essential foundation for moving forward to more advanced studies such as mapping melotte 72's vector field and analyzing its dynamical history. Moreover, a critical aspect of this work involves identifying factors contributing to the distorted shape using various cluster simulation models. Melotte 72's nearness to the Sun, 192 Myr old (Tasselli et al. 2019) binary system CPM 11330-205 ($1.081\pm.001$ kpc; Cinzano et al. 1999), and the presence of the galaxy's central disk field make it an ideal test case to examine the effects of the solar environment on melotte 72's star density distribution and the cluster's structural features. This study provides an essential groundwork to examine the relationship between the cluster's internal dynamics and the surrounding environment using various simulation models. Generally, adjusting the camera position involves moving it to specific marks on the object, however in this instance we explore the possibility of relocating the camera solely using image data, by translating or rotating the robotic arm. We introduce a new method, referred to as CLIC, where an artificial network processes an inspection image to generate required adjustments to be made to the camera, by translating these adjustments into a robotic movement command. We utilize a supplementary camera positioned outside the inspection area and, in combination with CLIC, are able to successfully teach the robotic arm these adjustments, by simulating inspection actions on a separate object. We demonstrate that this technique achieves highly accurate results on a dataset comprising 12 objects from the NIST-810 dataset and outperforms existing approaches (a conventional system where a 3D model is used) with significantly reduced computational complexity. Furthermore, we show that this technique achieves effective results on a few in-line inspection tasks developed within our laboratory. We believe that this type of technique has the potential to benefit a great deal of industrial applications where it's difficult or costly to build up 3D models of inspected objects. In constrained reinforcement learning, a RL agent receives an ideal policy. The goal is to find a state-action system that the agent believes to be optimal. We focus on the reverse version of this problem, where the state-action model is known, but the agent's perception needs to be simulated. The desired agent policy is specified as an optimization objective, with a constraint based on the perception loss. By using techniques like Lagrangian decomposition and entropy regularization, the computation can be efficiently reduced from NP-hard to NP-compatible or even NP-compatible itself. The method can effectively learn the desired agent's behavior in the StarCraft II Multi-Agent Learning Environment with improved results. It generally scales better than existing methods for large learning tasks. We also demonstrate its potential in generating diverse agent behaviors through an analysis of the environment's map design. We believe this approach has the potential to contribute to various fields, including social and artificial intelligence, by designing behaviors that align with the preferences of a central controller. We provide open-source code for the implementation.

The European Space Agency's GAIA space mission, scheduled to launch in 2013, will create detailed 3D maps of the Milky Way galaxy by measuring the positions and movements of approximately 500 million solar neighborhood stars over an extensive period. By utilizing these data and transforming them into celestial charts, researchers will investigate the galaxy's structure and evolution. With a payload consisting of a spin-scan telescope and on-board data processing capabilities, GAIA will generate 1% accurate distance measurements and mappings of the galaxy's star population across various regions. However, developing these products poses challenges due to inherent difficulties associated with processing the data. To address these issues, I will describe the mission's objectives and outline the methodology for creating the core products, before identifying the primary difficulties in executing these processes. Finally, I will present several alternative strategies for generating these products as part of the ongoing development efforts. By selecting these methods, the GAIA data products will undergo refinement through expert evaluation, resulting in delivery to researchers by 2016. The mission will then enter its observational phase, spanning approximately 4.9 years, during which it will produce transformed data. By utilizing these transformed products, researchers will have increased opportunities to explore the galaxy's structure and evolution in depth. The data will also be supplemented by various supporting products, made available to researchers through the 17,000 file database, comprising (1) raw data, (2) processed data, (3) scientific products, and (4) supporting information. By providing these transforming products, the GAIA mission will significantly expand the galaxy's 3D mapping capabilities, enabling researchers to push the boundaries of their investigations by approximately one decade. By enabling such advancements, the GAIA mission will have a profound impact on the development of future astrometric space missions, including those designed to chart nearby galaxies, the Milky Way's bulge and disk regions, and the entire local volume. Potentially, the GAIA data will also unlock new avenues for investigating various astrophysical phenomena and fundamental universal paradoxes, such as dark matter and star clustering, as well as the paradox of the birthplace of dark stars and the nature of the Galactic halo's global framework. By understanding these fundamental topics, the GAIA mission will significantly contribute to the advancement of the astrophysical and cosmological fields. However, to fully unlock its potential, the GAIA data will require transformation. By enabling such transformations, the GAIA data will become a powerful tool for advancing the fields of study and realizing the mission's full potential

For a given graph, we investigate the problem of identifying the minimum number of vertices required to split the graph into subgraphs with optimal treewidth for each part.  Treewidth is a crucial parameter used in graph algorithms and, therefore, finding vertex dividers has numerous applications.  Depending on the scenario, we propose two main approaches:  one focusing on minimizing the number of vertices when the treewidth values in each part are known beforehand, and another where the treewidth values are not initially known but can be determined during the process.  We establish that at least a certain fraction of these vertices belong to the dividers in the latter case.  Furthermore, we propose an algorithm and demonstrate its efficiency by showing it runs in specified time and space complexities.  The problem of finding the minimum number of vertices for the latter case remains unsolved but has been proven to be NP-hard when the treewidth values in each part are known beforehand, unless NP is equivalent to a uniform linear time system.  We also investigate the related problem of finding the minimum number of vertices for splitting the graph into subgraphs with optimal pathwidth and show that this problem remains NP-hard even under certain restricted conditions.  The study also examines the problem of identifying the minimum number of vertices for splitting the graph into subgraphs with optimal vertex elimination trees and shows that it remains NP-hard even for very restricted forms of these trees. This paper explores the 2008 algorithm by Rosenshtein-Kashuan, Pappalardo, and Vilenchik for identifying large groups of nodes in complex networks based on their connectivity. The method is particularly useful for analyzing networks that may not have clear-cut information about existing groups within the network. By applying weights to node connections, it's possible to distinguish between different types of links, which can then be used to refine the group structure. The approach is versatile and can be applied to various network types. However, it's crucial to note that this method is only effective for networks that have been somewhat organized or have existing groups, as it won't work for completely random or very tightly connected networks. To demonstrate its application, we used this method to analyze the Facebook social network, with results that made sense in the context of the group structure. Additionally, we explained how this method can be used to find node connections in networks where the information isn't available but can be inferred from existing connections. Lastly, we discussed some assumptions made in this method and suggested improvements for applying it to measured and heterogeneous networks. The growing presence of artificial neural networks in physics has brought concerns regarding the loss of explanatory capacity for these models. To address these issues and achieve an optimal balance between precision and comprehensibility, we suggest an underlying probabilistic framework for neural networks, which accounts for uncertainty throughout the training and prediction processes. This proposal is based on the concept of "credible regions," which allow us to set a specific threshold for prediction accuracy. To verify the validity of this approach, we create an artificial problem that mimics solving the Laplace equation in a complex environment with hidden inputs. Our model identifies a distribution that reduces to a Gaussian for simplified conditions, closely related to the finite element method. This approach was successfully tested in two complex conditions: a waveguide model and the Navier-Stokes equations. The results show that this method provides reliable and accurate error bars for the neural network's predictions, revealing how the training data influences the predictive distribution. This approach could serve as a starting point for building explanations for more complex models. Additionally, the most recent advancements in variational inference techniques could enhance the scalability of this method, allowing for the estimation of uncertainties in high-dimensional problems. Furthermore, this method could also expand to accommodate other physics-based loss functions. Our implementation of this approach can be found on our GitHub page at https://github.com/andreaspobitzer/CN. For visualizations, visit https://andreaspoblinger.github.io/CN. This work was supported by the Austrian Federal Ministry of Digital and Electrical Industries (BMDW) under the grant number 914279. The present paper represents the first publication supported by the grant, marking the beginning of a project aimed at integrating physics-based neural networks and the uncertainty quantification methods used in physics. The second publication in this series will focus on the optimization techniques front, while the third will cover uncertainty propagation. The third and final publication will delve into the verification and validation of these neural networks. This work is part of an interdisciplinary project aimed at understanding and applying the uncertainties present in real-world data to neural networks, an idea inspired by the work of J. R. Quinlan and M. L. Pino-Yates, demonstrating the value of uncertainty estimation for the interpretation of neural network predictions. We conduct a rigorous investigation of linear bandits, focusing on scenarios where actions are not simply basic vectors but rather complex, multi-dimensional objects like full matrices, highly-structured vectors, or specially constructed sets. The latter two action types are particularly practical as they significantly reduce the enormous dimensionality issues typically associated with traditional linear bandits. Our work emphasizes the importance of treating action subspaces as fundamental components of such scenarios. Based on these findings, we design highly efficient algorithms capable of each episode resolution in at most logarithmic time complexity, and efficient confidence intervals with a finite size and frequentist coverage rate of at least 95 percent, for all aforementioned settings. Furthermore, we establish some intriguing theoretical connections between the characteristics of action subspaces and sampling efficiency, also revealing that matrix-based actions offer particularly favorable conditions with significant implications for related multi-armed bandit problems. Additionally, we provide an alternative, cross-validation-inspired approach to linear bandits with rich action subspaces that might be of independent interest. Lastly, we demonstrate how the theoretical contributions of our work apply to a selection of practical, fully-observable motion planning use cases. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that theoretical guarantees have been provided for linear bandits with rich action sets. Such theories, previously available only for basic action vectors, have been found inadequate. As a direct result of our investigation, we are able to draw new, actionable conclusions regarding the properties of average and optimal action vectors, as well as to improve the existing theoretical frameworks of linear bandits. Moreover, we are able to show that the proposed matrix-based approach to linear bandits with efficient each-episode resolution and confidence intervals has a direct, promising impact on related motion planning use cases. Ultimately, we are able to show that the proposed algorithms are much simpler than those suggested in the most advanced prior bases. Deep learning methods employing graph convolutional networks achieve great success in processing data with graph structures. Graph convolutional networks are widely used in applications involving structural information. Current methods rely heavily on assumption of clean structural data. In real-world scenarios, this data is often compromised due to malware and forgery, resulting in malicious graph node insertion and removal. Consequently, graphical convolutional networks face significant challenges in such instances of data contamination. Diverging from standard deep learning approaches with simultaneous learning of both model and adapter, we instead adopt a reinforcement learning strategy for learning an adapter separately. Our adapter is then combined with a graph convolutional network trained through a backpropagation algorithm. This process is repeats for multiple iterations. This study introduces the GCDRC, a novel adapter learning approach. Our adapter is configured as an inverse graph transformation that maps the adapter's output to the original graph and then performs a reconstruction of removed nodes. This study introduces the NodeRCDRC as well as contamination assessment protocols to evaluate an adapter's efficacy. Our experiments utilizing synthetic and real-world datasets show that our approach outperforms existing methods in contamination-assisted performance. Furthermore, our approach performs comparably to models with no contamination but with a significantly reduced number of parameters. This leads to implications of achieved performance relative to exposure of the adapter during training. This study marks the first instance of using reinforcement learning for adapter learning in graph-based data. Our approach of learning an adapter through reinforcement is groundbreaking and opens doors for future research. This study is available on arXiv, with the arXxid:2103.15052 ID. We introduce OntoPlot, a novel visualization designed for visualizing connections between related concepts in extensive knowledge graphs. Distinguishing it from other tools, OntoPlot is particularly suited for visualizing extensive relationships within large ontologies like DOLN, DOJO, and YAGO, rather than focusing solely on smaller datasets. OntoPlot's capability to detect and display associations between groups of concepts within large datasets enables users to gain further insight into hidden connections among related concepts. Notably, we have found that these associations often adhere to a hierarchical pattern. Building on this discovery, we developed an adaptive visualization that caters to user needs at different scales, seamlessly transitioning from detailed plots of individual concepts to summary views of more extensive relationships. Furthermore, we have developed an automated system for identifying and prioritizing concepts based on their relevance to user queries, ensuring that users remain informed throughout their exploration of the visualizations. The effectiveness of OntoPlot has been validated through experiments using DOLN, DOJO, and YAGO, which demonstrate its capacity to facilitate user comprehension and provide accurate information. We anticipate that OntoPlot will serve as a valuable discovery tool for domain experts seeking to identify patterns within these datasets and contribute to the expansion of these ontologies through new, related concepts. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss strategies, namely CycleGAN and Pairwise Loss, to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. In standard end-to-end ASR training, a model is typically fine-tuned using a speech-text loss function in an autoregressive manner. To leverage unlabelled speech data more effectively, we propose integrating a speech-domain-aware loss, which compares the generated speech with its real counterpart after undergoing a sophisticated speech-to-spectrogram transformation. Notably, we found that utilizing the Pairwise Loss yields better ASR performance than the more computationally intensive Spectrogram Matching Loss. Moreover, we demonstrated that the combination of end-to-end and inter-domain losses can significantly boost end ASR performance. Experimental evaluations on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal that the proposed method achieves a 5-10% relative improvement in categorical error rate compared to conventional models. Notably, we achieved a 4.7% relative error reduction over the LibriSpeech test clean benchmark. To facilitate reproducibility, we make our code and model configuration available for download at: https://github.com/IndigoVL/LGSS_ASR end-to-end model. A crucial task in intelligent security systems, pedestrian detection is challenging due to the vast scale and diversity of pedestrian data. Domain gaps between pedestrian datasets and target domains significantly affect the detection's accuracy. Existing domain adaptation techniques primarily focus on improving the model's representation or loss function without directly addressing the abundance and diffusion of pedestrian data. As a result, they struggle with false positives in target domains. To address this issue, we present a novel unsupervised false positive reduction method called Box Re-Ranking, which combines with domain adaptation. Our method groups box features into multiple subsets, represents each subset with distinct embedding channels, and uses a decision-free loss to perform target domain box re-ranking. This approach effectively reduces false positives and improves domain adaptive pedestrian detection. Experiments on the Waymo Open Perception Challenge and Citypersons dataset demonstrate that our method achieves a mean average precision rate of 10-20% higher than state-of-the-art domain adaptive pedestrian detection methods. The goal of this research is to explore advanced techniques for enhancing music quality. We investigated the application of multiple music improvement networks in a end-to-end system, which was trained to minimize perceived distortion in music quality after modification. However, our findings indicate that using an image translation network alone to preserve original audio features results in minimal improvements. To overcome this limitation, we introduced a new network architecture that combines the capabilities of a generator, responsible for maintaining original melody, and a vocoder, responsible for synthesizing the modified music pitch. We discovered that using an image translation network in conjunction with the generator and vocoder combination yields significantly improved results. Specifically, we observed that the combined system produces more natural full-band music with clearer melody lines. We observed notable performance enhancements from our approach in various music transformation tasks, including pitch shifting, vibrato application, and chord extrapolation. Notably, the distilled knowledge extracted from the image translation process helps a vocoder to accurately generate original melody lines in modified music. This research lays the groundwork for uncovering music generation challenges and identifying new approaches to enhance music quality through various advanced network architectures. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on observers' perception of a throw. To achieve this goal, we created a simulation tool that allows users to simulate ball paths according to various throwing techniques and points of release, using anthropomorphic 3D models. Through a study involving over 60 participants who provided force and velocity estimates for virtual ball catches, we identified key insights from our experiment: participants tend to correct their estimates in response to apparent (visible) points of release, even if the virtual ball path is generated randomly; to determine the apparent point of release, observers consider both the ball's trajectory and speed; incorporating visual cues of the thrower's body helps participants accurately judge the point of release. Our research discovered that artificial (artfully generated) paths that suggest a ball released low and behind a thrower are more convincing than paths that suggest a ball released high and ahead of the thrower, regardless of the actual point of release chosen. Our research indicates that throwing motions featuring virtual ball paths that appear to have the thrower's body and suggest the ball was released low and behind typically evoke the fewest incorrect force and velocity estimates from observers. These findings are relevant to researchers working on the application of simulated throwing motions in forensic and forensic intelligence systems. We suggest constructing multiple paths for each throw type that are designed to be realistic, rather than aiming to simulate the physics of throwing accurately. By utilizing these simulated paths, the system can select the path that appears most plausible to the user. To address the goal of accurate simulation, our research reveals a need to investigate the impact of the thrower's visual presence on the perception of throwing motions. Ultimately, our research suggests the need for further investigation into the specific features of realistic throwing motions and the impact of the thrower's visual presence, in order to develop a thorough understanding of the factors influencing the perception of throws. Our research was presented at the CHI 2022 conference. A substantial amount of information in the scientific community originates from data analysis involving the comparison of individual items and collective groups. Examples include the relationship between the sizes of particles, the distribution of frequencies and durations of occurrences, and the differences between successive individual values and group-averages. Many of these examples can be described using multiplicative stochastic processes, where the multiplication factor represents an interaction between individual items and the growing collection. Theoretical research has primarily focused on the characteristics of such processes under specific assumptions, such as independence and identical distribution of the multiplicative factors. Our study instead explores the properties of a multiplicative process with a sample-dependent lower bound, potentially applied to scenarios like the analysis of fellow-traveling phenomena where small positive deviations from an average value are common. Theoretical findings are further substantiated by numerical simulations using three distinct examples: the growth of pulmonary nodules, the differences between successive values in the Financial Time Series, and the durations of reigning movie box office chart-tops. The research demonstrates a set of moment estimates for the multiplicative process, along with a method to infer the underlying distribution of multiplicative factors. The proposed approach has been compared with alternative distribution-free estimators and shown to produce accurate results in the three case studies. The theoretical framework is also expected to be applicable to other distribution-free methods for analyzing growth data. The estimated distributions of multiplicative factors can be utilized for different purposes, such as the practical application of the Kolmogorov-Rao test for detecting outliers, the regression analysis between growing quantities and their growth patterns, and the calculation of return times on financial time series. The theoretical and numerical outcomes of this research provide valuable insights for scientists and practitioners aiming to analyze data describing the relationship between individual items and collective groups using multiplicative stochastic processes. The associated R software package'mutprocess' implements the proposed ideas and empirical results. The package can be installed using the command 'install.packages("mutprocess")' and run with the command 'library(mutprocess)'; all examples can be replicated with the provided 'data(fellowTraveling).R' data and'mutfit()','mutsim()', 'kolmogtest()','retTime()' functions. The software also includes additional tools for analyzing growth data as described in the related study listed in Ref. [30]. We introduce a family of random Clifford circuits with remarkably low depth, 
allowing us to compute shadow states at a fraction of the cost compared to standard circuits. Leveraging this advantage, we're able to cast an eye over the performance of various neural-superconducting-qubit architectures by analyzing the average similarity between states that should be identical, a metric we term expectation alignment. Through this analysis, we're able to evaluate the efficacy of different parameterization approaches, including both standard and real-time quantum associative memory formulations. By leveraging our shallow shadow technique, we're able to assess the performance of these architectures with minimal computational overhead, revealing some notable trends in their behavior. Specifically, we find that the memory capacity of qfm-QAM increases in a linear manner with the number of qubits, whereas regular QAM appears to experience a decline in its effective qubit count as more layers are added. This disparity highlights the expectation alignment benefits of using low-depth shadow circuits in multi-layered quantum systems. Building upon the concept of representation learning, we investigate whether popular techniques can automatically discover effective representations that facilitate generalization across different tasks. Through theoretical examination, we identify a specific scenario - linear transformations within the multi-layer neural network framework - that allows us to prove both the feasibility of discovering these representations without supervision and the necessity of having an unsupervised discovery method. Furthermore, we establish that using these learned representations in conjunction with a simple query-efficient optimization method leads to query-efficient transfer capabilities among a wide range of tasks, notably minimizing the need for new training on the task of predicting the mean of a given dataset. To validate our theory, we develop Demonstrable, a novel unsupervised learning method for discovering linear representations that outperforms traditional baseline methods. When combined with optimization methods for predicting the mean, we achieve significant improvements, retrieving only a small percentage of the total data as opposed to nearly half of the total data by the baseline method. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/keziheplef/demonstrable.

The detection of pneumonia through automated computer processing has garnered significant attention due to its potential to alleviate the disease's severity. However, creating high-quality automated annotations for chest X-rays is a labor-intensive task, leading to limited data availability. As a result, there's a need to explore more efficient methods of obtaining annotations to support automated pneumonia detection. We investigated the potential of augmenting data to reduce the necessity for labelled data in automated pneumonia detection. Specifically, we evaluated the effectiveness of automatic boundary prediction using unet++ on augmented images from the RSNA detection challenge dataset. Boundaries obtained from augmented, unlabelled images were used in models performing detection and classification on the challenge dataset. Results indicated a recall of 65% for the full dataset and a 57% recall for the challenge's validation dataset, both obtained using augmented, unlabelled images. Furthermore, we established that the most beneficial augmentations for automated boundary prediction were image rotation and addition of Gaussian noise. While still outperformed by trained medical experts, our approach demonstrates the feasibility of using augmented, unlabelled images to reduce data requirements for automated pneumonia detection. As a result, this technique holds potential for broader applications in automated medical image analysis. To tackle this issue, we focus on fine-tuning a pre-trained T5 model, which is typically used for generating text in a general setting, by incorporating image-specific features and promoting creativity in image description. We demonstrate that our approach effectively leverages object mentions to enhance image description quality. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the prompts to provide deeper insights into the characteristics of the model's generated image descriptions. Our findings and resources will facilitate future research in this domain. The proposed method is available at https://github.com/NTU-NLP/PROMT.

Our research introduces zero-shot voice translation, which enables translation without language overlap using utterance-level acoustic features as input signals. We develop a direct end-to-end model framework that processes these acoustic features to produce translated utterances in a target language, bypassing the need for pre-existing translation datasets in that language. We identify three key challenges in this area: insufficient signal quality, translation accuracy, and coherence. To address these issues, we create a significant, signal-quality-enhanced dataset for zero-shot voice translation and develop two cutting-edge models. We conduct comprehensive experiments on three languages and assess different signal representations from raw waveforms to articulatory features through both objective and subjective evaluations. The results show that our proposed approach significantly surpasses existing benchmark models in both translation accuracy and coherence. Moreover, we create a new dataset with zero-shot translation parallelism and demonstrate that our model produces translated text with minimal edits from human editors. The corresponding codes and dataset are available at https://github.com/baileysteine/ZS-VT.git, with the dataset being updated regularly. Our research contributes to zero-shot voice translation and lays the groundwork for cross-language, zero-shot voice translation models. It also sheds light on signal representation for translation, and the importance of improving translation coherence in translation evaluation. Importantly, our study reveals that translation performance is hindered by poor signal quality, emphasizing the need for signal enhancement in translation. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to explore signal enhancement in translation. Finally, our model has the potential to facilitate zero-shot voice translation in translation-dependent languages by leveraging existing monolingual datasets. The model is also compatible with other languages that lack pre-existing translation datasets in the field of statistical machine translation. Accurate low voltage network load forecasting is crucial to inform decision-making and ensure the efficient operation of the distribution sector. We present a probabilistic model designed for daily load peaks at the low voltage level, and a comprehensive dataset featuring real and forecasted load profiles for the UK's distribution network between 2020 and 2021. Our model demonstrates improved forecasting capability when incorporating a wide range of time-of-use data and neighboring time-step information, and we observe statistically significant correlations within time-of-use data. We demonstrate that integrating model predictions with historical forecasts from various sources enhances overall prediction accuracy. Furthermore, utilizing a Bayesian hierarchical model with shifted and scaled distributional priors allows our model to effectively estimate daily peaks and output probabilistic forecasts consistent with empirical observations. During evaluation, our model's probabilistic predictions consistently surpass those of a reference Bayesian hierarchical model with shifted and scaled reference distributions centered around naive forecast assumptions. We observe that incorporating model predictions from a wide range of sources leads to a 10.6% improvement in mean absolute error (MAE) over the naive approach. Furthermore, our model's probabilistic predictions demonstrate the potential to facilitate reliable peak demand forecasting and contingency planning for the low voltage grid, and we observe a 11.6% reduction in MAE when modeling outages at 10-20 times the nominal level is sufficient to capture observed outage rates. With outage models intact, we find that incorporating model predictions from a wide range of sources leads to a 9.8% improvement in mean absolute error (MAE) compared to the naive approach. We anticipate that our probabilistic forecasts and methods will play a significant role in informing decision-making and ensuring contingency planning for the low voltage grid. Our code is available upon request for academic purposes. We propose that incorporating model predictions from a wide range of sources could facilitate reliable forecasting and decision-making across a variety of applications. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the potential for model and forecast aggregation to enhance forecasting capability and provide a platform for robust decision-making. We anticipate that similar approaches could be developed to support decision-making in other areas, and we encourage industry stakeholders and academic researchers to explore a wider range of forecast aggregation methods to further mitigate forecast uncertainty. Our research suggests that incorporating model predictions from a wide range of sources could play a significant role in addressing the challenges of unreliable forecasts and communication during distribution and retail levels. We propose that standardizing communication protocols for the sharing and aggregation of distribution-level model predictions could significantly improve forecasting accuracy and facilitate reliable decision-making. Our code is available upon request for academic purposes.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications, including radiation therapy and bone disease diagnosis. Current efficient methods use 3D CNNs to generate a vertex map from which the vertebrae centers are detected through optimization. Nevertheless, these centers are often inaccurately localized, leading to identification failures in complex cases. To address this issue, we introduce Spine-Loc, an automated vertebrae localization system that leverages customized loss functions and post-processing to improve both translation and rotation robustness. By introducing a rectified spine strategy, the system adapts to different vertebral shapes. Anatomically-constrained optimization is employed to boost performance in challenging cases. Experiments on large, public datasets showcase the superior accuracy of our approach compared to existing methods, particularly in localizing vertebrae of unusual shapes. Achieving consistent results across the full spine is a notable feat. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/BIISys/SpineLoc, supplemented by our pre-trained models. The fixed-suspension design of traditional quadruped robots restricts their lower limbs, making it beneficial to incorporate flexible actuation in gait generation. This research focuses on the development of supple quadruped robots featuring flexible actuation in three of its legs. We leverage reinforcement learning, coupled with a custom dense reward scheme, to train these robots. Our approach to reward distribution enables quadruped robots to learn a range of gaits that optimize a variety of performance metrics. Experimental results on the Sinki quadruped demonstrate that the elastic actuation enhances maximum speed by 11.7%, offering an advantage in mobility over conventional actuation. Furthermore, the elastic actuation improves the robot's resistance to unexpected disruptions, boosting its tolerance by 52.4%. This study also explores the trade-offs between actuation flexibility and other performance metrics that are affected by this design choice. We ultimately provide a design guide to help engineers determine when the benefits of flexible actuation are necessary. This research ultimately aims to expand our understanding of the role that actuator elasticity plays in quadruped locomotion, setting the stage for the development of flexible suspension systems in quadruped robots. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance capabilities. The integration of new standard technologies, such as IEEE 802.11k/v, presents an opportunity to significantly enhance wireless networks' efficiency. By enabling more precise control, these technologies allow for a more strategic use of available WiFi channels. However, optimal channel allocation is complicated by the dynamic nature of home networks, as well as the varying quality of different wireless channels. In order to improve home network performance, it is crucial to maximize network throughput and minimize interference between adjacent access points. To achieve this, we propose AP/Extender Selection: a novel method for selecting and configuring WiFi channels within home networks. By strategically selecting and configuring AP/Extenders to take advantage of IEEE 802.11k/v's feedback mechanisms, we can effectively improve home network performance. The proposed method achieves this by dividing and allocating high-quality wireless channels to each AP/Extender, thus preventing interference and maximizing throughput. In situations involving high WiFi load levels, the proposed method is shown to significantly outperform traditional strategies, improving overall home network throughput by up to 25% or better. Similarly, the proposed method is shown to outperform traditional strategies in scenarios where WiFi channels are subject to high levels of interference, improving throughput by up to 30% or better under such conditions. The proposed AP/Extender Selection method utilizes IEEE 802.11k/v's feedback mechanisms to identify and avoid such interference, thus taking into account the quality of different wireless channels when selecting and configuring AP/Extenders. By employing this approach, the proposed method is shown to be applicable across a range of realistic WiFi load levels and channel quality scenarios.
